  1. [MATH: f(x+\pi) = f(x)] for all [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}]

  2. [MATH: f(x) = F(x)] for all [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}]

1. [MATH: f(x+\pi) = f(x)] for all [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}]
2. [MATH: f(x) = F(x)] for all [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}]
3. [MATH: f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = f(x)] for all [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Since [MATH: f] is the [MATH: \pi]-periodic extension of [MATH: F,] we have

  • [MATH: f(x+\pi)=f(x)] for all [MATH: x\in\mathbb{R},] and

  • [MATH: f(x)=F(x)] for all [MATH: x\in[0,\pi).]

With that in mind, we examine each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of [MATH: \pi]-periodicity: [MATH: f(x+\pi)=f(x)] for all [MATH: x\in\mathbb{R}.]

  • Statement II is true. Notice that [MATH: F] itself is [MATH: \pi]-periodic, because for any [MATH: x\in\mathbb{R},] we have [MATH: F(x + π) = \cos (2(x + π)) = \cos (2x + 2π) = \cos (2x) = F(x).] Since [MATH: F] already satisfies the periodicity rule, the [MATH: \pi]-periodic extension agrees with [MATH: F] everywhere, so [MATH: f(x)=F(x)] for all [MATH: x\in\mathbb{R}.]

  • Statement III is false. For example, take [MATH: x=0.] Then,

[MATH: f(x + (π)/(2)) = f((π)/(2)) = F((π)/(2)) = \cos (π) = − 1,] while [MATH: f(x) = f(0) = F(0)\cos (0) = 1.] Hence, [MATH: f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \neq f(x)] for [MATH: x=0.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only".

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we will represent a [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic function [MATH: f(x)] as an infinite sum of simple sine and cosine waves. This representation is called the Fourier series for [MATH: f(x)]:
[MATH: f(x)\sim \frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big)]
The key idea is that we can "build" a complicated periodic graph by adding together basic waves. For example, below we have a discontinuous periodic function approximated by the first few terms of its Fourier series.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dd8d954f57a40344107408873f488516]

Content:
This gives us a powerful way to analyze periodic behavior by breaking it down into simple oscillations. Fourier series play a central role in modeling vibrations, signals, and other repeating patterns.

Content:
To work with Fourier series, we typically start with a function defined on a single base interval, such as [MATH: [-\pi,\pi),] and then extend it to be periodic over all real numbers. This process creates what is called a periodic extension.

Content:
In the next slide, we will define this concept formally and look at some examples.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Periodic Extensions

Content:
Recall that a function [MATH: f(x)] is [MATH: p]-periodic if [MATH: f(x+p)=f(x)] for all [MATH: x\in\mathbb{R}.]

Content:
Now, if [MATH: F(x)] is defined on an interval [MATH: x \in [a,b)] of length [MATH: p,] then its [MATH: p]-periodic extension [MATH: f] is defined by the two properties:

Content:
- [MATH: f(x+p)=f(x)] for all [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}]
- [MATH: f(x)=F(x)] for all [MATH: x \in [a,b).]

Content:
For example, let [MATH: F(x) = -x] be defined on [MATH: x\in [0,2).] Now, suppose [MATH: f(x)] is the [MATH: 2]-periodic extension of [MATH: F(x)] from [MATH: x\in [0,2)] to [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}.] The graphs of [MATH: y=F(x)] and [MATH: y=f(x)] are shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9fb8a259022c1450df8b28f36b9bc6c5]

Content:
Watch out! We should always be aware of the difference between [MATH: F(x)] and its extension [MATH: f(x).] For instance, consider the function [MATH: F(x)=2\sin(x)] defined on [MATH: x \in [0,\pi)] and its [MATH: \pi]-periodic extension [MATH: f(x).] The graphs of [MATH: y=F(x)] and [MATH: y=f(x)] are shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/dca63a920b41ca81d4fbb2063e7b9efb]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: f(x)] is not just [MATH: 2\sin(x)!] But it would coincide with [MATH: 2\sin(x)] if we were to consider the [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension of [MATH: F(x)=2\sin(x)] from, say, [MATH: x \in [0,2\pi]] to [MATH: x \in \mathbb{R}.]

---

Item 3 — Example: Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function

Item 6 — Tutorial: Reminder: Orthogonal Functions

Content:
Recall that we can define an inner product on functions over [MATH: [-\pi,\pi)] given by
[MATH: \langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.]
Also recall that functions [MATH: f] and [MATH: g] are called orthogonal (with respect to this inner product) if [MATH: \langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=0.]

Content:
The key fact we will use throughout this lesson is that the functions
[MATH: 1,\ \cos(x),\ \sin(x),\ \cos(2x),\ \sin(2x),\ \ldots]
are orthogonal with respect to the inner product defined above.

Content:
More precisely, for integers [MATH: m,n\ge 1,] we have the following orthogonality relations on [MATH: [-\pi,\pi)]:

Content:
- [MATH: \langle \cos(mx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0] if [MATH: m\ne n,]
- [MATH: \langle \sin(mx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0] if [MATH: m\ne n,] and
- [MATH: \langle \sin(mx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0] for all [MATH: m,n.]

Content:
Also, the constant function [MATH: 1] is orthogonal to every sine and cosine:

Content:
- [MATH: \langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle=0,] and
- [MATH: \langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle=0] for all [MATH: n\ge 1.]

Content:
Finally, we will also use the squared norms of these functions:
[MATH: \langle 1,1\rangle=2\pi,
\quad
\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle=\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle=\pi
\quad
\text{for all } n\ge 1.]

Content:
Let's see how this works in concrete examples.

Content:
Note: Both intervals [MATH: [-\pi,\pi)] and [MATH: [0,2\pi)] are considered standard in this context. We’ll use [MATH: [-\pi,\pi)] in tutorials, but some exercises use [MATH: [0,2\pi).]

Item 10 — Tutorial: Fourier Series Form For 2pi-Periodic Functions

Content:
Recall that we are considering a [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic function [MATH: f(x)] that is piecewise continuous on [MATH: [-\pi,\pi).] We can represent [MATH: f(x)] by its Fourier series:
[MATH: f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big).]
Our goal is to find the formulas for the coefficients [MATH: a_0, a_n,] and [MATH: b_n.]

Content:
To do this, we'll use a powerful idea from linear algebra. We define an inner product for functions on the interval [MATH: [-\pi,\pi)] as
[MATH: \langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.]
With this inner product, the set of functions [MATH: \{1, \cos(nx), \sin(nx)\}] for [MATH: n\ge 1] is an orthogonal set.

Content:
This means we can think of the Fourier coefficients as projections of the function [MATH: f(x)] onto each of these orthogonal "directions". The coefficients [MATH: a_0,a_n,b_n] simply tell us "how much" of [MATH: f(x)] lies in each of these directions.

Content:
On the next slide, we will use this idea to derive the formula for the first coefficient, [MATH: a_0.]

Item 11 — Tutorial: The Formula For the Constant Term

Content:
Let's derive the formula for the coefficient [MATH: a_0] by taking the inner product of the entire Fourier series
[MATH: f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big)]
with the constant function [MATH: 1.]

Content:
- Step 1. Start with the Fourier series and take the inner product of both sides with [MATH: 1{:}]
[MATH: \langle f(x),1\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big),\,1\right\rangle]
- Step 2. Use the linearity of the inner product to distribute it across the sum:
[MATH: \langle f(x),1\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,1\rangle
+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\langle \cos(nx),1\rangle
+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} b_n\langle \sin(nx),1\rangle]
- Step 3. Apply the orthogonality property. For any [MATH: n\ge 1,] we have [MATH: \langle \cos(nx),1\rangle=0] and [MATH: \langle \sin(nx),1\rangle=0.] This makes all the terms in the sums equal to zero:
[MATH: \langle f(x),1\rangle=\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,1\rangle]
- Step 4. Solve for [MATH: a_0.] We just need to calculate [MATH: \langle 1,1\rangle=\displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} 1\cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x=2\pi.]
[MATH: a_0=\dfrac{2\langle f(x),1\rangle}{\langle 1,1\rangle}
=\dfrac{2\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cdot 1\,\textrm{d}x}{2\pi}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\,\textrm{d}x]

Content:
We find the formulas for [MATH: a_n] and [MATH: b_n] (for [MATH: n\ge 1]) in a similar way.

Content:
- To find [MATH: a_n,] we take the inner product of the Fourier series with [MATH: \cos(nx).] By orthogonality, the only term that is not zero on the right-hand side is the one involving [MATH: \langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle.]
[MATH: \langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle = a_n \langle \cos(nx), \cos(nx)\rangle]
Since [MATH: \langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}\cos^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x = \pi,] we can solve for [MATH: a_n{:}]
[MATH: a_n = \dfrac{\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle}{\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\,\textrm{d}x]
- Similarly, to find [MATH: b_n,] we take the inner product with [MATH: \sin(nx){:}]
[MATH: b_n = \dfrac{\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle}{\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,\textrm{d}x]

Content:
Note: If [MATH: f] is the [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic extension of a function [MATH: F] defined on [MATH: [-\pi,\pi),] then we can replace [MATH: f(x)] with [MATH: F(x)] inside the integrals.

Content:
Now that we have the formulas for all the coefficients, let's work through a concrete example.

For a [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic function [MATH: f(x)] that is piecewise continuous over [MATH: x\in [0,2\pi),] the Fourier series of [MATH: f] is given by

Item 15 — Tutorial: Deriving the Formulas For the Fourier Coefficients

Content:
Once again, recall that we are considering a [MATH: 2\pi]-periodic function [MATH: f(x)] that is piecewise continuous on [MATH: [-\pi,\pi).] We represent [MATH: f] by its Fourier series
[MATH: f(x)\sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\big(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\big).]

Content:
To determine the coefficients, we use the inner product on [MATH: [-\pi,\pi)]:
[MATH: \langle f(x), g(x)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x.]

Content:
We have already seen the derivation for the coefficient [MATH: a_0] early in the lesson.

Content:
Now, we derive the formula for [MATH: a_n] for [MATH: n\ge 1{:}]

Content:
- First, we take the inner product of both sides with [MATH: \cos(nx){:}]
[MATH: \langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\big(a_k\cos(kx)+b_k\sin(kx)\big),\,\cos(nx)\right\rangle.]
- Using linearity, we get
[MATH: \langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k\langle \cos(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} b_k\langle \sin(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle.]
- By orthogonality, [MATH: \langle 1,\cos(nx)\rangle=0,] [MATH: \langle \sin(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0] for all [MATH: k,] and [MATH: \langle \cos(kx),\cos(nx)\rangle=0] whenever [MATH: k\ne n,] so
[MATH: \langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle=a_n\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle.]
Since [MATH: \displaystyle \langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \cos^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x=\pi,] we obtain
[MATH: a_n=\dfrac{\langle f(x),\cos(nx)\rangle}{\langle \cos(nx),\cos(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(nx)\,\textrm{d}x.]

Content:
Finally, we derive the formula for [MATH: b_n] for [MATH: n\ge 1{:}]

Content:
- First, we take the inner product of both sides with [MATH: \sin(nx){:}]
[MATH: \langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle
=
\left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\big(a_k\cos(kx)+b_k\sin(kx)\big),\,\sin(nx)\right\rangle.]
- Using linearity, we get
[MATH: \langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle
=
\dfrac{a_0}{2}\langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k\langle \cos(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle
\!+\! \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} b_k\langle \sin(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle.]
- By orthogonality, [MATH: \langle 1,\sin(nx)\rangle=0,] [MATH: \langle \cos(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0] for all [MATH: k,] and [MATH: \langle \sin(kx),\sin(nx)\rangle=0] whenever [MATH: k\ne n,] so
[MATH: \langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle=b_n\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle.]
Since [MATH: \displaystyle \langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle=\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin^2(nx)\,\textrm{d}x=\pi,] we obtain
[MATH: b_n=\dfrac{\langle f(x),\sin(nx)\rangle}{\langle \sin(nx),\sin(nx)\rangle}
=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin(nx)\,\textrm{d}x.]

Content:
Putting these together, the Fourier coefficients are the following:
[MATH: a_{0}|= (1)/(π)∫_{− π}^{π}f(x)dx; a_{n}|= (1)/(π)∫_{− π}^{π}f(x)\cos (nx)dx, n ≥ 1; b_{n}|= (1)/(π)∫_{− π}^{π}f(x)\sin (nx)dx, n ≥ 1]
